claims.claim: Human population is distributed very unevenly across Earth; people cluster together rather than spreading evenly, and roughly two-thirds of the world's population lives within three large clusters centered on East Asia, South Asia, and Europe.
Arithmetic density is the number of people in an area divided by the total size of that area.
Physiological density is the number of people per unit of arable (farmable) land, and it better reflects population pressure on food-producing land than arithmetic density does.

For the United States, arithmetic density is about 32 people per square kilometer, while physiological density is about 179 people per square kilometer, because only a relatively small share of US land is arable.
People do not live uniformly across the world but in clusters shaped by Earth's physical geography; environments that are too dry, wet, cold, or mountainous act as limiting factors on settlement.
Carrying capacity is the number of people (or organisms) an environment can support given available resources; it is a central concept in discussions of population and resources.
Population density is commonly measured and mapped as the number of people per square kilometer of land area, using United Nations population estimates over land-area figures.
World population reached 8 billion people on 15 November 2022 and is projected by the UN to peak at around 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources differ on how many major population clusters to name and whether Southeast Asia and eastern North America count as top-tier clusters.
positions: The Oklahoma State OER and National Geographic describe three great clusters (East Asia, South Asia, Europe) holding about two-thirds of humanity.
Some texts add Southeast Asia and eastern North America as secondary or fourth-ranked clusters.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names the three principal clusters (East Asia, South Asia, Europe) as the well-established core, and mentions Southeast Asia and eastern North America as smaller secondary clusters, without asserting a single fixed count.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft treated 'population distribution' as an abstract organizing label with no geographic content, no clusters, no density measures, and no data. None of that boilerplate was usable as evidence.
